judge_assessment.explanation: Every value the judge lists reproduces. f(-1) = |-1-3|+2 = 6; the table f(0), f(3), f(7) = 5, 2, 6; g(-9) = 2|-9+4|-5 = 2(5)-5 = 5; p(-2) = 3(-2)+1 = -5 and p(2) = 2^2-3 = 1 because the top branch carries x < 2; C(4) = 4+3(4-1) = 13; q(-3) = -(-3)-1 = 2, q(0) = 0^2 = 0, q(1) = 4-1 = 3 since the third branch owns x >= 1; |x-3|+2 = 6 gives x = -1 and 7; C(3.5) = 4+3(2.5) = 11.5 and 4+3(t-1) = 16 gives t = 5; and 3x+1 = x^2-3 gives x^2-3x-4 = 0, so (4,13) and (-1,-2). The judge's manual-review note on item 9 is also exact: p(2) = 1 by the condition x >= 2, and the two branch formulas differ there by 7 - 1 = 6, which is the six-unit jump. Absolute-value order of operations is handled correctly throughout (problem 3's hint 'the bars close before the multiplying starts' is the right warning for 2|x+4|-5), and the guide has rules, examples and distinct try-its. My partial disagreement is about the prompt's closing clause, 'clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review'. Problem 10 asks two things - find every point where the two branch formulas agree, AND 'say whether either of those inputs is a place where p itself would be continuous, and why'. The answer key answers the second half well ('Neither point makes p continuous ... p only switches branches at x = 2, and 2 is not one of these two inputs'), but verify.json id 10 is a single system entry covering only the intersection points, with no manual entry, so the sheet's hardest conceptual question is recorded as fully machine-verified and the Quick Answers row reads '10. x = 4, y = 13, x = -1, y = -2' with no marker. Two smaller slots are also unbound: problem 2 says 'mark the three points on the graph in the Function Reference and check that they land on the V' (a marked representation with no manual entry), problem 4 says 'name the branch you used and say which condition made you pick it' for each of two evaluations, and problem 6 says 'say which one sits exactly on a boundary, and which branch its condition sends you to'. Problem 9 is flagged correctly and is the only manual entry in the file.

strengths_to_preserve: The Function Reference panel on page 1 defines f, g, p, q and C once and every problem points back to it, so ten problems exercise five functions instead of introducing ten. That reuse is what makes the later items possible: the student evaluates p in problem 4, is asked to diagnose the same p's boundary in problem 9, and then dissects the same p's two branch formulas in problem 10. The concept accumulates on one object.

The parking model C(t) is deliberately built so the flat branch and the linear branch agree at t = 1 (both give 4), which makes it the continuous foil to p's six-unit jump. That contrast is the whole point of problems 9 and 10 and it is designed into the reference panel rather than asserted in the key.

Problem 3's hint states the operator-precedence trap in the exact terms it occurs: 'the 2 multiplies the absolute value, so the bars close before the multiplying starts', and verify.json declares the matching trap (2*(x+4)-5, the bars dropped) so the wrong path is a checked object.

Problem 9 is flagged manual with a desc that states all three things a reader must find - why the formulas differ at x = 2, which value the definition selects, and what the graph does there - rather than a bare 'explanation, review by hand'. That is the right level of instruction for a hand grader.

root_causes.description: Manual flagging was applied at the problem level rather than the slot level: problem 9 is entirely open so it got a manual entry, while problems 10, 4, 6 and 2 mix a machine-checkable half with an open half and were classified by their machine-checkable half alone. Because the contract requires only one check per problem id, an id whose system entry verifies is reported as covered and the conceptual half disappears from both the gate summary and the Quick Answers bank.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 10: 'Find every point (x, y) where the two formulas produce the same output. Then say whether either of those inputs is a place where p itself would be continuous, and why.' verify.json id 10 is one system entry with expected [{x:4,y:13},{x:-1,y:-2}] and no manual entry.

answer_key.pdf devotes a full paragraph to that second half ('Neither point makes p continuous, and the reason is the conditions'), so the author knew it was a separate, open response and still did not declare it.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '9. -' for the correctly flagged manual item but '10. x = 4, y = 13, x = -1, y = -2' with no marker for the partly open one.

worksheet.pdf problem 2 asks the student to 'mark the three points on the graph in the Function Reference and check that they land on the V'; verify.json id 2 has three eval entries and no manual entry, though SKILL.md line 257 lists marked and drawn representations as manual.
worksheet.pdf problems 4 and 6 each require the student to name the branch and the condition that selected it; neither id carries an entry for that.

improvements.title: Flag the open half of mixed items, starting with problem 10's continuity question and problem 2's marked points
improvements.proposed_change: Apply the open-response gate per response slot rather than per problem, so an id that already carries a machine entry is still failed when one of its printed slots is an explanation, a diagnosis or a marked or drawn representation. For this sheet that means adding a manual entry under id 10 whose desc states what a reader should find (neither (4,13) nor (-1,-2) is a switch point of p, whose only switch is x = 2, so the agreement is arithmetic that p never uses) and a manual entry under id 2 for the three points marked on the reference graph. Then have render_quick_answers.py append the manual marker to any row whose id mixes machine and manual entries, so row 10 reads with the marker rather than looking fully checked.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: curr-296's problem 10 prose bound to a verify.json id holding only the system entry. The slot-level open-response gate must exit non-zero naming the unflagged continuity question. Adding a manual entry under id 10 must make it pass, and the rendered bank row must then carry the manual marker alongside the four coordinate values.
improvements.expected_impact: Delivers the prompt's labelling clause on the item that most needs it - the sheet's synthesis question, whose conceptual half is the only part not reducible to a solve. It also fixes a misleading grading page where the fully manual item 9 and the half-manual item 10 look categorically different when they are not.
improvements.risk: Slot-level flagging will materially raise manual counts on concept-model sheets where most items pair a computation with a justification, so the gate summary needs to separate 'manual by design' from 'unverifiable by accident' or the metric will read as a regression.

improvements.title: Bind the branch-and-condition naming slots in problems 4 and 6
improvements.proposed_change: Count each conjoined request inside a sub-part as its own response slot and require a binding. Problem 4 asks for p(-2) and p(2) AND, for each, the branch used and the condition that selected it; problem 6 asks for three values AND which input sits on a boundary and where its condition sends it. The cheapest correct binding is a condition-check entry type: declare the interval condition alongside the eval (for id 4's second entry, that x = 2 satisfies x >= 2 and fails x < 2) so branch selection becomes a verified fact rather than an assertion in the key. This is the same gap the canonical verify-conditions-not-just-values key describes, applied to branch naming that the worksheet explicitly asks the student to write down.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: curr-296's problem 4 prose ('(a) Find p(-2). (b) Find p(2). For each one, name the branch you used and say which condition made you pick it') with the two existing eval entries. The slot gate must exit non-zero naming the two unbound branch-naming slots. Adding condition declarations to each eval must make it pass and must make the bank row show which condition each value came from.
improvements.expected_impact: Branch selection is the declared focus of this sheet, and it is currently verified only implicitly by the choice of expr the author typed. Declaring the condition catches the exact author error the worksheet is teaching against - evaluating a boundary input with the branch whose condition excludes it.
improvements.risk: Condition checking needs interval arithmetic for the general case and will need to degrade to manual on conditions the parser cannot evaluate; a silent pass on an unparsed condition would be worse than the present gap.

case_summary: A polished and exact concept-models packet on evaluating absolute-value and piecewise functions. I re-derived all sixteen machine results independently - 6; 5, 2, 6; 5; -5 and 1; 13; 2, 0, 3; -1 and 7; 11.5 and 5; and the intersections (4,13) and (-1,-2) - with no discrepancy, and confirmed the judge's item-9 reading that p(2) = 1 with a six-unit jump. The design deserves the score: one Function Reference panel supplies five functions that the ten problems reuse, so problem 4 evaluates the same p that problem 9 diagnoses and problem 10 dissects, and the parking model is deliberately built continuous at its breakpoint to act as the foil for p's discontinuity. The gap is that manual flagging was applied per problem instead of per slot. Problem 9 is fully open and correctly flagged; problem 10 is half open - 'say whether either of those inputs is a place where p itself would be continuous, and why' - and carries only a system entry, so the sheet's hardest conceptual question shows on the grading page as fully machine-checked. Problem 2's marked points and the branch-naming requests in problems 4 and 6 are unbound for the same reason.
